analysis.one_liner: Repeals the Dodd-Frank law that regulates Wall Street banks and protects consumers.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or vote: it was referred to the Senate Finance Committee on the day it was introduced and died there when the 114th Congress ended in January 2017.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would erase the Dodd-Frank Act, the sweeping 2010 law passed after the financial crisis. Repeal would remove the consumer bureau that polices credit cards and mortgages, the rules requiring big banks to hold more capital, oversight of the derivatives market, and the government's power to wind down a failing financial firm without a taxpayer bailout. It would put Wall Street back under roughly the pre-2008 rulebook. The bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee on January 7, 2015, and no further action was ever taken on it.
analysis.who_benefits: Large banks and other financial firms benefit, because they would be freed from the capital requirements, derivatives oversight, and consumer-protection rules imposed after the 2008 crisis. Financial executives and shareholders gain if relaxed regulation raises profits.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Large Wall Street banks and financial firms

how_it_helps.text: The bill repeals the Dodd-Frank Wall Street Reform and Consumer Protection Act in full and revives the laws as they stood before it was enacted.

Repeal would lift the post-crisis rules on banks — including capital standards, derivatives-market regulation, and the new consumer financial protection bureau — returning the financial sector to the pre-2008 regulatory regime.

analysis.who_pays: Ordinary consumers and taxpayers bear the cost. Consumers would lose the dedicated watchdog over mortgages, credit cards, and loans that Dodd-Frank created, and taxpayers would again stand behind a financial system with fewer safeguards against the kind of failures that forced bailouts in 2008.

drawbacks.text: Repeal would eliminate the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau created by Dodd-Frank, leaving consumers without that dedicated agency policing mortgages, credit cards, and other consumer financial products.

Repeal would remove Dodd-Frank's order to restore pre-crisis law as if the Act had never passed, stripping the capital requirements, derivatives rules, and wind-down authority enacted in response to the 2008 crisis.

Without those safeguards, the risk of bank failures large enough to again require taxpayer support returns to the pre-2008 level; this was the core argument against repeal and the reason Dodd-Frank was enacted.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The gains would flow almost entirely to large financial firms through lighter regulation, while the costs — weaker consumer protection and higher systemic risk borne by taxpayers — fall on the public. There is no significant consumer-side offset in the bill; it is a straight repeal with no replacement provisions.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced and never got a hearing, a markup, or a vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. David Vitter introduced the bill on January 7, 2015, with one Republican cosponsor.
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance.
No further action appears in the bill's history: it never received a committee hearing, a markup, or a floor vote, and it died when the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Ordinary consumers and taxpayers are better off because the bill died — they kept the post-crisis bank rules and the consumer financial watchdog. Large banks did not get the repeal they would have gained from it.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Consumers and taxpayers kept the bank rules

for.name: Sen. David Vitter
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to repeal Dodd-Frank in full.

against.name: Senate Committee on Finance
against.what_they_did: Received the referral and took no action — no hearing, markup, or vote — for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was sponsored by two Republicans and drew no Democratic support; oversight of Wall Street banks split largely along party lines in this era.

industries.note: Full repeal of Dodd-Frank would free the biggest banks from post-crisis capital rules, oversight, and wind-down authority, raising their flexibility and profitability while shifting the risk of failures back onto taxpayers. Consumers would simultaneously lose the dedicated financial products watchdog the law created.
Repeal would remove Dodd-Frank's regulation of the derivatives market, which was a central unregulated force in the 2008 crisis, letting dealers return to pre-crisis practices.
Eliminating the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau by repealing Dodd-Frank would remove federal oversight of mortgages, credit cards, and consumer loans, freeing lenders from that policing.
